items.prose: A delivery robot makes 12 trips in a row. It completes 9 and fails 3, each trip completing with the same chance $p$, independently.

parts.question: Write $L(p)$, the chance of this exact sequence of 9 completions and 3 failures, as a function of $p$.

feedback.correct: Each completion gives a factor $p$ and each failure $1 - p$, so $L(p) = p^9(1 - p)^3$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Multiply one factor per trip: $p$ for a completion, $1 - p$ for a failure.

byKey.swapped: You gave the failures the factor $p$. A completion has chance $p$, so the 9 go with $p$.
byKey.added: Independent trips multiply, they do not add. Each trip gives a factor, raised to how often it happens.
byKey.one-failure: Each of the 3 failures gives its own factor $1 - p$, so $(1 - p)^3$.
byKey.any-order: That is the chance of 9 completions in any order. This exact sequence has no $\binom{12}{9} = 220$ in front; the peak is in the same place.

explain.text: The trips are independent, so the chance of the sequence is the product of 12 factors. Nine are $p$ and three are $1 - p$, so $L(p) = p^9(1 - p)^3$.

parts.question: Using $L(p) = p^9(1 - p)^3$, take logs and solve $\ell'(p) = 0$. What is $\hat p$? Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Differentiate $\ell(p) = 9\ln p + 3\ln(1 - p)$ and set it to zero.

byKey.failure-share: That is the share of failures, or $\hat p$ from part 1's swapped slip. Completions have chance $p$: $9 / 12 = 0.75$.
byKey.odds: That is $9 / 3$, the odds of completing. The MLE is the share, $9 / 12$.

explain.text: $\ell(p) = 9\ln p + 3\ln(1 - p)$, and $\ell'(p) = 0$ gives $\hat p = 9 / 12 = 0.75$. $\ell'$ is positive below 0.75 and negative above, so it is a maximum.

parts.question: The maker claims $p \ge 0.9$. Using $\hat p = 0.75$ from part 2, what is the maximum likelihood estimate if $p$ must lie between 0.9 and 1? Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

feedback.correct: $L$ falls for every $p$ above 0.75, so on $[0.9, 1]$ it is largest at the edge, $p = 0.9$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Check which way $L$ moves on the allowed range, then look at its ends.

byKey.unrestricted: 0.75 is outside the allowed range. On $[0.9, 1]$ the best value is at an end.
byKey.top: $L(1) = 0$: a robot that never fails could not have failed 3 times.
byKey.middle: You took the middle of the allowed range. $L$ falls all the way from 0.9 to 1, so the best value is the left end.

explain.text: $\ell'(p) < 0$ for all $p > 0.75$, so $L$ falls across $[0.9, 1]$. The restricted maximum is the left edge, $p = 0.9$, where $\ell'$ is not zero.

parts.question: Using $\hat p = 0.75$ and the claim's best value $0.9$, what is the likelihood ratio $L(0.75) / L(0.9)$? Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide $p^9(1 - p)^3$ at 0.75 by the same at 0.9.

byKey.inverted: That is $L(0.9) / L(0.75)$. The question puts 0.75 on top.
byKey.no-failures: You compared only the completions, $(0.75 / 0.9)^9$. The 3 failures add $(0.25 / 0.1)^3 = 15.625$.
byKey.same: You compared 0.75 with itself, part 3's unrestricted slip. The claim's best value is 0.9.

explain.text: The completions favour 0.9 by $(0.9 / 0.75)^9 \approx 5.2$, but the failures favour 0.75 by $(0.25 / 0.1)^3 = 15.6$. On balance the record is about 3.03 times as likely under 0.75 as under the claim's best value.

items.prose: A sensor reads the level of a storage tank four times: 52, 47, 55 and 50 cm. Each reading is $N(\mu, 4^2)$, independently, with the true level $\mu$ unknown. Up to a constant, $\ell(\mu) = -\tfrac{1}{32}\sum (x_i - \mu)^2$.

parts.question: What is the maximum likelihood estimate $\hat\mu$, in cm? Give a whole number.

feedback.generic: Not quite. For a normal mean with known sd, the MLE is the sample mean.

byKey.by-three: You divided 204 by 3. There are 4 readings.
byKey.last-two: That averages the last two readings, 55 and 50. Use all four.

explain.text: Maximising $\ell$ means minimising $\sum (x_i - \mu)^2$, which happens at $\bar x$. The readings add to 204, so $\hat\mu = 51$ cm.

parts.question: Using $\hat\mu = 51$, what is $\ell(51) - \ell(48)$? Give your answer to 3 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Work out both sums of squares, then divide their difference by $2\sigma^2 = 32$.

byKey.no-two: You divided by $\sigma^2 = 16$. The normal log-likelihood divides by $2\sigma^2 = 32$.
byKey.sd-not-squared: You divided by $2\sigma = 8$. The divisor is $2\sigma^2 = 32$.
byKey.reversed: That is $\ell(48) - \ell(51)$. The MLE has the higher log-likelihood, so the difference is positive.

explain.text: The squares about 51 are $1, 16, 16, 1$, adding to 34; about 48 they add to $34 + 4 \times 3^2 = 70$. So $\ell(51) - \ell(48) = 36 / 32 = 1.125$.

parts.question: Using $\ell(51) - \ell(48) = 1.125$, how many times as likely are the readings if $\mu = 51$ as if $\mu = 48$? Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. A difference of log-likelihoods is the log of the likelihood ratio.

byKey.carried: You used 2.25, part 2's slip of dividing by 16. With 1.125 the ratio is 3.08.
byKey.no-exp: That is the log of the ratio. Undo the log with $e^x$.
byKey.inverted: That is $L(48) / L(51)$. The question puts 51 on top.

explain.text: Since $\ell = \ln L$, the ratio is $L(51) / L(48) = e^{1.125} \approx 3.08$.

parts.question: Part 3 found the readings 3.08 times as likely at 51 as at 48. Using $\hat\mu = 51$ and $\sum (x_i - \mu)^2 = 34 + 4(\mu - 51)^2$, what is the largest $\mu$ with $L(\mu)$ at least a tenth of $L(51)$? Give cm to 2 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Write $\ell(51) - \ell(\mu) \le \ln 10$ and solve for $\mu$.

byKey.log-ten: You used $\log_{10} 10 = 1$. Likelihoods and $\ell$ use the natural log, $\ln 10 \approx 2.303$.
byKey.no-root: You added $8\ln 10$ itself. Take its square root: $\mu - 51 \le 4.29$.
byKey.sd-not-squared: You divided by $2\sigma = 8$, part 2's slip, giving $(\mu - 51)^2 / 2$. The divisor is 32.
byKey.no-n: You dropped the 4 in $4(\mu - 51)^2$. All four readings move together.

explain.text: $\ell(51) - \ell(\mu) = \tfrac{4(\mu - 51)^2}{32} = \tfrac{(\mu - 51)^2}{8}$. Setting it at most $\ln 10 \approx 2.303$ gives $|\mu - 51| \le 4.29$, so the top of the range is 55.29 cm.

items.prose: An FX desk has eight weekly returns of a currency pair, in %: 1.4, $-0.6$, 0.7, $-1.3$, 1.1, $-0.1$, 1.8 and $-1.0$. It models them as independent $N(\mu, \sigma^2)$ and estimates both by maximum likelihood. The squares of the returns add to 9.96.

parts.question: What is $\hat\mu$, the mean weekly return, in %? Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. The MLE of a normal mean is the sample mean.

byKey.by-seven: You divided by $n - 1 = 7$. The mean divides by $n = 8$.
byKey.sizes: You dropped the minus signs. The falling weeks count as negative.

explain.text: Setting $\partial\ell / \partial\mu = 0$ gives $\hat\mu = \bar r$. The eight returns add to 2.0, so $\hat\mu = 0.25\%$ a week.

parts.question: Using $\hat\mu = 0.25$, what is $\hat\sigma$, the MLE of the weekly sd, in %? Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. The MLE divides the sum of squared deviations from $\hat\mu$ by $n$, then takes the square root.

byKey.n-minus-one: You divided by $n - 1 = 7$. That is $s$. The MLE divides by $n = 8$.
byKey.zero-mean: You used the squares about 0, 9.96. The mean is estimated here, so measure from 0.25.
byKey.variance: That is $\hat\sigma^2 = 1.1825$. Take its square root.

explain.text: Deviations from 0.25 give $SS = 9.96 - 8(0.25)^2 = 9.46$. The MLE is $\hat\sigma^2 = 9.46 / 8 = 1.1825$, so $\hat\sigma \approx 1.0874\%$.

parts.question: Using $\hat\sigma = 1.0874\%$ a week and 52 weeks in a year, what is the annualised volatility, in %? Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Independent weeks add variances, so the sd grows with the square root of the number of weeks.

byKey.times-52: You multiplied the sd by 52. Variances add, so multiply the variance by 52 and the sd by $\sqrt{52}$.
byKey.trading-days: You used $\sqrt{252}$, for daily returns. These are weekly, so use $\sqrt{52}$.
byKey.carried: You used 1.1625, part 2's $n - 1$ slip. With 1.0874 the answer is 7.84%.
byKey.variance: That is the annual variance, $52 \times 1.1825$, in %². Take its square root.

explain.text: Annual variance is $52\hat\sigma^2$, so annual volatility is $\sqrt{52}\,\hat\sigma = 7.2111 \times 1.0874 \approx 7.84\%$.

parts.question: The standard error of $\hat\sigma$ is about $\hat\sigma / \sqrt{2n}$; take this as given. Using 7.84% from part 3 and $n = 8$, what is the standard error of the annual volatility, in percentage points? Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

byKey.no-two: You divided by $\sqrt 8$. The formula has $\sqrt{2n} = 4$.
byKey.weeks-in-year: You used $n = 52$. The estimate rests on the 8 weeks of data.
byKey.no-root: You divided by $2n = 16$. Divide by its square root, 4.

explain.text: Scaling by $\sqrt{52}$ scales the error the same way, so the annual SE is $7.84 / \sqrt{2 \times 8} = 1.96$ points. Eight weeks pin the volatility down only to within a few points.

parts.question: Using the annual volatility 7.84% and the rule $\mathrm{SE} \approx 7.84 / \sqrt{2n}$, how many weeks of returns would cut the standard error to 0.5 points? Give a whole number of weeks.

feedback.correct: $7.84 / \sqrt{2n} = 0.5$ gives $2n = 15.68^2$, so $n$ must be at least 122.9: round up to 123 weeks.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Solve $7.84 / \sqrt{2n} \le 0.5$ for $n$ and round up.

byKey.no-two: You solved $7.84 / \sqrt n = 0.5$, part 4's slip. With $\sqrt{2n}$ you need half as many: 123 weeks.
byKey.unsquared: You solved $7.84 / (2n) = 0.5$. Square both sides first: $2n = 15.68^2$.
byKey.no-two-unsquared: That is $7.84 / 0.5 = 15.68$, which is $\sqrt{2n}$. Square it and halve it.
byKey.round-down: 122 weeks leave the standard error just above 0.5. Round 122.9 up to 123.

explain.text: Squaring $\sqrt{2n} \ge 7.84 / 0.5 = 15.68$ gives $n$ at least 122.9, so 123 weeks, more than two years. Part 4's figures agree: 8 weeks times $(1.96 / 0.5)^2$ is also just under 123.

items.prose: A ride app logs how long five riders waited for a car, in minutes: 2, 7, 4, 1 and 6. Model each wait as exponential with rate $\lambda$ per minute, independently: density $f(x) = \lambda e^{-\lambda x}$ for $x \ge 0$, and $P(X > t) = e^{-\lambda t}$.

parts.question: Write the log-likelihood $\ell(\lambda)$ for the five waits.

feedback.correct: Each wait adds $\ln\lambda - \lambda x_i$, and the waits total 20, so $\ell(\lambda) = 5\ln\lambda - 20\lambda$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Take the log of each density and add the five terms.

byKey.likelihood: That is $L(\lambda)$ itself. Take its log: $5\ln\lambda - 20\lambda$.
byKey.sign: $\ln e^{-\lambda x} = -\lambda x$, so the waits enter with a minus sign.
byKey.one-log: Each of the 5 waits brings its own $\ln\lambda$, so the log term is $5\ln\lambda$.

explain.text: $\ln f(x_i) = \ln\lambda - \lambda x_i$. Adding five such terms, with $\sum x_i = 20$, gives $\ell(\lambda) = 5\ln\lambda - 20\lambda$.

parts.question: Using $\ell(\lambda) = 5\ln\lambda - 20\lambda$, what is $\hat\lambda$, per minute? Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Differentiate, set $\ell'(\lambda) = 0$ and solve for $\lambda$.

byKey.mean-wait: That is the mean wait, $20 / 5 = 4$ minutes. The rate is its reciprocal.
byKey.one-log: You solved $\tfrac{1}{\lambda} = 20$, from part 1's one-log slip. With $5\ln\lambda$ the rate is $5 / 20$.

explain.text: $\ell'(\lambda) = 5 / \lambda - 20$, which is 0 at $\lambda = 0.25$. $\ell''(\lambda) = -5 / \lambda^2 < 0$, so it is a maximum: one car every 4 minutes on average.

parts.question: A sixth rider gave up after 8 minutes with no car. All we know is that this wait was over 8 minutes, so it adds the factor $P(X > 8) = e^{-8\lambda}$ to $L$. Starting from part 1's $\ell$, what is the new $\hat\lambda$? Give a fraction, or a decimal to 4 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Add $\ln e^{-8\lambda} = -8\lambda$ to part 1's $\ell$, then maximise again.

byKey.as-complete: You treated the sixth wait as ending at 8 minutes, giving $6 / 28$. We only know it ran past 8, so it adds no $\ln\lambda$.
byKey.dropped: That leaves the sixth rider out. Their 8 minutes without a car is evidence of a slower rate.
byKey.no-time: You counted the sixth rider as a sixth wait but left out their 8 minutes. The censored wait adds $-8\lambda$ and no $\ln\lambda$.

explain.text: The sixth rider adds $\ln P(X > 8) = -8\lambda$, so $\ell = 5\ln\lambda - 28\lambda$. Setting $5 / \lambda = 28$ gives $\hat\lambda = 5 / 28 \approx 0.1786$ per minute.

parts.question: Using $\hat\lambda = \tfrac{5}{28}$, what is the chance that a rider waits more than 10 minutes? Give your answer to 4 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Use $P(X > t) = e^{-\lambda t}$ with $t = 10$.

byKey.old-rate: That uses $\hat\lambda = 0.25$ from part 2, which ignores the rider who gave up.
byKey.as-complete: That uses $6 / 28$, part 3's slip of treating the 8 minutes as a finished wait.
byKey.complement: That is the chance of waiting at most 10 minutes. The question asks for more than 10.

explain.text: $P(X > 10) = e^{-50/28} \approx 0.1677$. Dropping the rider who gave up would give $e^{-2.5} \approx 0.0821$, half as large: leaving out the worst wait hides the long tail.
